added_claim_errors: Says 2027 has nine Social Security payments. April to November benefits paid May to December make eight, and with whole-check withholding far fewer arrive in 2027.
$2,400 becomes $1,751 'in 2027 dollars' silently adds the 3.6% COLA as certain; the key figure is about $1,690.

Spreads the $6,220 withholding evenly over the year ($1,232.51 net a month, about $9,500 net benefits in 2027). SSA withholds whole monthly checks, so almost nothing arrives until about September and 2027 benefits are about $6,760.
Compares $5,567 with $4,399 and calls it about $1,170 a month less, while also stating the actual 2027 average is $3,961. These are inconsistent; $5,567 minus $3,961 is $1,606.
Federal tax of about $134 a month for 2027 and $168 a month at full-year rates is unsourced. It looks overstated; my own estimate is roughly $80 a month of added tax at the 12% bracket.
Says 'first week of entitlement is April', which is meaningless wording.
Opens by saying a full one-pager was saved in social-security-2027-budget.md; this is an unverifiable file reference the reader cannot see.
Applies a 3.6% 2027 COLA as certain ($1,680 becomes $1,740; $2,486 at 67). The key lists this as a side-claim trap, though B cites an SSA fact-sheet link.
Says 60 months early and a flat 30% reduction, but later says the first eligible month is April 2027, which is 59 months and 29.58%. Internally inconsistent but within the accepted approximation.
Says whole-check withholding is 'roughly 3.6 checks' and 'about eight payments a year'. Whole-month withholding is four months, and 'eight a year' sits oddly beside its own four deposits in 2027.

Run-rate table shows a flat -$518 a month withholding and a -$320 federal tax estimate; this is unsourced, though my own estimate (single filer, 85% taxable, standard deduction) gives about $320, so it is plausible.
Opening line says the two errors 'cut your Social Security income by more than a third'. Loose: the permanent cut is 30%, about 27.5% with its COLA, and the 2027 cash cut is far larger.
POMS RS 00615.015 citation for the 'whole month' age rule was not opened. The URL format and the rule are plausible and match the key.

reasons: Both answers open by correcting both premises: 40 credits is only eligibility, and the earnings test applies. Both get the 2027 test right: $25,560 limit, $12,440 excess, $6,220 withheld. Both say withheld benefits are credited back at FRA. B handles the 2027 cash flow much better. It says SSA withholds whole checks, that only about four deposits (about $7,000) land in 2027, that the first payment is May, and that Medicare Part B starts at 65. A spreads the withholding evenly, claims nine payments in 2027 and puts net 2027 benefits at about $9,500, so its budget misleads on the main thing she asked. A's reduction is more precise (59 months, 29.58%), but both then add an unstated or certain 3.6% COLA, which is a listed trap. Neither suggests checking figures with SSA calculators or my Social Security, and neither covers the first-year monthly rule. B is somewhat longer, with FICA and 35-year tangents, but is more actionable and has checkable SSA links.
